title: How are people solving long-term memory/coherence in AI RPGs?
author: NovelFlame_AI
selftext:
Has anyone else building AI-driven RPGs/story systems noticed how predictable the “memory collapse curve” starts becoming after a while?

In chapters 1-3, everything feels incredible. Characters remember details, relationships feel reactive, choices feel meaningful, and the world feels alive.

By chapters 4-6, small inconsistencies start creeping in. Someone references the wrong event, a character’s personality drifts slightly, a rivalry loses tension, and the AI starts smoothing over unresolved emotions because it wants scenes to remain conversationally coherent.

By chapters 7-10, the story is still technically readable, but emotionally it starts feeling weirdly hollow. Characters stop carrying emotional weight forward properly, betrayals lose consequences, promises evaporate, and everybody slowly converges toward the same conversational cadence/personality. The world stops feeling shaped by accumulated history and starts feeling more like a sequence of locally-generated scenes.

I honestly think this is where a lot of AI story/game systems quietly break immersion even when the prose itself is decent.

What’s interesting is that players usually do not point at the exact technical issue either. They just start saying things like “the characters stopped feeling real” or “the story lost something.”

Curious how other people building in this space are handling it. Structured memory? Character-state systems? Relationship tracking? Summarization layers? Manual authorial intervention? Ancient forbidden technologies lol?

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body: Don't rely on LLM context windows or the LLM at all for this. Do what you can to feed it all of the information it needs each turn and track that information elsewhere.

replies.author: Mobile_Bonus4983
replies.body: I do the opposite. But I don't load a lot of lore into the context window, only history and gm-prompt. I track how well the LLM knows the campaign material (World of Darkness, D&D, etc). It works fine enough.

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body: That works until it doesn't.

replies.author: Mobile_Bonus4983
replies.body: Seems true for all models. But yes. I usually don't play long play.

replies.author: Mobile_Bonus4983
replies.body: I used claude when it was cheap and abundant with a json and lore, recent exchanges, etc and it worked out great. But quite expensive!

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: Yeah....maybe not treating the LLM itself as the source of truth and more like a renderer sitting on top of structured state

replies.author: Arkanta
replies.body: Oh yeah you definitely need a structured engine that uses the LLM as a tool to help with narration etc. You can't take the hands off the wheel!

comments.author: Revolutionary_Heart6
comments.body:
im no pro. but i think creating some database tracking certain important stuff and always impacting them when they must be impacted could work. also using an actual map that can be traveled.

and the map avoid you being able to say "i walk up to the volcano"

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: This is actually a really interesting way to think about it, thank you. I keep focusing so much on emotional continuity that I sometimes forget how important physical/world consistency is for contributing to the overall continuity and making the world seem real, an actual place instead of existing scene-to-scene.

replies.author: Revolutionary_Heart6
replies.body: Glad i could help. i hope that help you achieve what youre looking for :)

comments.author: orblabs
comments.body: I am building something like that, and actually started building it because something as Silly Tavern was really cool but couldn't hold up a real play session due to the reasons you highlighted. The solution is a lot of harness work, assemble action specific context, have the LLM use tools and request informations when it needs it, evaluate the output, and another ton of little tricks and attentions. I am very happy of where i am now, but holy hell it has been a long voyage ...

comments.author: leather-armor
comments.body: I've been having some success with context-specific pgvector storage. Social facts go into one place and can then be looked up by vector similarity, and the results have been surprisingly good thus far.

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: Smart! I always feel like relationship memory is the most important to interactive fiction players, and where they're the least forgiving of inconsistencies

comments.author: loopywolf
comments.body:
If this is ANY help, I recently mentioned memory incoherence to a collegue as I was working with a board game design and he said "at the end of a session , ask the AI to summarize all the key points in a markdown file." You then reload this when you start another session.

Then, last week I asked AI to run a Dune 2d20 RPG game for me and used this technique and not only has it retained coherence and memory, it is *the* most incredible RPG experience I've had as a player.

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: The “session summary” trick works way better than people expect! I think players are surprisingly forgiving of compressed memory as long as the emotional continuity survives.

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
I’m still messing with it. Tricky balance of traditional code and llm. My first attempts the code was way too tight, llm was too boxed into creating dialogue and scenes that I could have just prewritten, way too much resource use not enough creativity. middle attempts too loose, exactly what ur describing. 

What i learned is, the llm needs very specific instructions on tone or the characters get very same-y and what to talk about or the llm just asks the player to drive the action. 

What i am going to try next is using an agent or feeding in a part of the prompt that has a function that evaluates how close the proposed dialogue is to the description of the character, if it falls below a threshold, then refeed the prompt with reminder. 

Tough balance between constantly feeding in all the character info and overloading rhe llm with information it needs to parse but not use, and giving it just what it needs to keep it from screwing up.

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: The “characters slowly becoming the same person” problem is so REAL lol. I kept noticing that once emotional continuity weakens, the model starts converging toward the same conversational rhythms because that’s the statistically safest place for it to go.

replies.author: 0bscuris
replies.body:
I asked the llm how to solve it and what it basically said was, you need to double check me and when you notice a character going same-y, remind me to see how they r supposed to be. If you have multiple characters, ask it would this other character say that? And if the answer is yes, do something different.

Now the problem with llm solutions is that they don’t care about resource, the answer is always more context. If it was left up to the llm they would have so much context it couldn’t process it’s own solutions. 

But, that doesn’t mean there isn’t a good idea buried under a terrible execution. 

Using llm is like herding an animal, if you don’t let it have space to move around, it’s a miserable experience, if you let it do whatever it wants, it shits in the garden. The traditional code builds the fence, the llm plays inside. Sometimes you gotta show it the fence so that it doesn’t run too far afield.

comments.author: HipHopperChopper
comments.body: Writing should not be done by AI. Organized yes, help flesh out? Sure. But it should be almost entirely authored and reviewed in depth by human hands. AI does not have the ability to properly develop a meaningful story in my opinion. If you want something players will connect to, you're going to have to write it.

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: I actually think this is closer to collaborative systems design than “replace writers” tbh. IF/game systems seem to get much stronger once humans are designing the structure, constraints, memory systems, pacing, character state, consequences, etc. and the AI is operating inside that framework instead of just 100% replacing it. Best experiences I’ve seen feel less like “AI wrote a novel” and more like collaborative narrative systems.

comments.author: Former-Objective-272
comments.body:
I hit this exact wall building a narrative roguelite where NPCs remember the player's actions across multiple lifetimes. The LLM context window approach collapsed around chapter 4 every single time.

What ended up working for me:

1. External state store. I keep a structured JSON log of every significant player action (killed NPC X, stole item Y, revealed secret Z). This is the source of truth, not the LLM context.

2. Pre-injection filtering. Before each NPC interaction, the system queries the state store for relevant memories (same NPC, same location, same faction) and injects only those into the prompt. Not the full history. Relevance scoring is rule-based with a simple recency decay.

3. NPC knowledge asymmetry. Different NPCs have different access to the memory store. The town drunk might only remember that someone matching your description was here last week. The spymaster remembers exact dialogue. This asymmetry makes the same memory store feel much deeper than it actually is.

The key insight: the LLM should generate the surface text, not manage the state. Treat the LLM like a rendering engine, not a database.

comments.author: Mobile_Bonus4983
comments.body:
I've been playing around with building my own. I generally rely on the level of context window for the LLM. Most models are around 200k context window and a short campaign will make do with that. I put all memory in json and have one process that prunes that file for things that gets old or log parts that aren't important anymore. 

Having a solid 1M context window with a cheapish model that do role play will be the best option. GLM5.1 does role playing fine enough. 

I don't use vector/db because its too expensive when not using LLM locally.

comments.author: quiqly_1
comments.body:
Yeah, for longer-term memory I’ve actually found plain text context, Obsidian-style vaults, organized .md files, structured notes is quietly beating RAG in a lot of these cases. The retrieval step is where so much breaks: chunking destroys relational context, embeddings collapse semantic nuance, and the model ends up reasoning over a partial slice of what it actually needed. Whereas if you just dump organized markdown into context, the model sees the whole graph and can reason across it. Token budgets keep expanding too, so the brute-force “give it everything relevant” approach keeps getting more viable.

But you’re right that it’s fragile either way. The core problem you’re describing isn’t really a memory architecture problem it’s a verification problem, which I think would need to be a Ground truth system/api that the game engine exposes.

Like you said, on long horizon I think LLMs like fundamentally struggle with time. So if you say X event happened 45 minutes ago, which should be important for the next interaction, it has a really hard time organizing thoughts temporally, which I think is leading towards the slow degrading of quality and thoughtfulness.

I think what works best is ground truth will still fully come from the game engine, and then the LM is just wrapping that ground truth in fancier, high definition dialogue. 

Need to mess with this more because it’s a super big framework that I think many games will have to deal with.

replies.author: NovelFlame_AI
replies.body: True that a lot of emotional drift is not even factual forgetting, it’s the model slowly losing its sense of which past events are still emotionally “active” in the story versus which ones can fade.

comments.author: Former-Objective-272
comments.body:
Mobile_Bonus4983: I use a local SQLite database for the state store, queried by simple key-value lookups (NPC_id + event_type). No LLM needed for retrieval. The relevance filtering is a deterministic rule engine with a recency decay weight. The LLM only sees the filtered result injected into its prompt.

For cost: the LLM call is the expensive part, not the db query. A SQLite lookup is microseconds. The key is doing the filtering BEFORE the LLM call so you minimize token usage. Each NPC interaction in my game uses ~200-400 tokens of injected context, not the full history.

NovelFlame_AI: Thanks! The asymmetry idea came from noticing that in real life, different people remember the same event completely differently. The town drunk remembering 'someone was here' vs the spymaster remembering 'a figure in a blue cloak asked about the magistrate at midnight' makes the world feel lived-in. It is also a great optimization trick.

comments.author: flawovpa
comments.body: not directly building an rpg system but i ran into the same collapse pattern using eroplay for long running scenarios, and what helped was leaning hard into their scenario builder to pre-anchor character goals and relationships before the session even starts. when the AI has a defined role and motivation baked in from the beginning it drifts way less than freeform chat. still not perfect past like 8 or 9 exchanges but the structured scaffolding buys you a lot more coherent mileage than just winging it.
